job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at 6:40 and take the bus to a small surveying and civil design firm in Hull. I started there four months ago as a graduate technician on a one-year contract. Mostly I check drawings against site measurements and fix small errors in the drawing software, and my line manager Pete (my supervisor) signs it off. I like the days when I'm out on a site with the survey crew. I hate the afternoons when I sit at a screen correcting the same kind of mistake forty times. I share a rented flat with two other people, and the rent plus my loan repayments eat most of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say good, because most of the hype has been noise so far. At work I'd tell Pete that the software's auto-checker saves us a few minutes and that's it. To friends I'd say I'm glad nothing's collapsing, because I've got enough going on. Online I'd just argue that if employers want less work done by people, they should pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing improves for me. I passed my degree with an average mark, I had no internship, and I owe a huge amount. If nothing changes, then I just stay on this contract and hope Pete renews it in the spring. I'm scared that if they don't, there are hardly any civil jobs around here. That worry is there with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to work and keep my head down. I'd put away maybe £40 a month if I can, because I've got under a month of rent saved. I'd also join the union branch for engineering staff, because I think a contract like mine needs someone behind it. I wouldn't touch AI tools, since I never have and I don't see why I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels flat, a bit grey. Not scary like the other pictures, but I'm already tired. It's like waiting for a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money worry is there with or without AI. What's the first bill that goes unpaid if the contract isn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My share of the rent is the big one, so I'd be calling my landlord, a man called Mr Keane, and begging for a month. I'd put the loan on hold, which the loan company allows but charges for in the end. I'd never skip the electricity because my flatmate Dan (my housemate) would notice at once. So rent first, loan second, and I'd be signing on for benefits within a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union, if your own job isn't under threat from AI in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the threat is the contract, not the machine. Fixed-term deals let a firm drop a person quietly in spring and nobody notices. Our firm has eleven staff and no union at all, so if I started a branch I'd be the person they'd remember when renewals come. I know that's a risk, and I'm still thinking about it.

say: I'd say good, **nothing** collapses, and employers should still pay for training.
I'd tell Pete (my supervisor) the auto-checker saves minutes, not jobs.
think: Off the record, I fear my **contract** won't be renewed, with or without AI.
I owe a **huge debt** and have under one month of rent saved.
do: Keep working the contract and save about **£40 a month**.
Ask the engineering union about joining a **branch** for staff on short contracts.
Keep **avoiding** AI tools, as I always have.
feel: Flat and tired, like waiting for a **bill** I know is coming.
S0.quote: The threat is the contract, not the machine. Fixed-term deals let a firm drop a person quietly in spring and nobody notices.
fieldNote: His worry is the **contract**, not AI, which shows in how quickly he turned to rent and loan details.
Union thinking comes from his politics and from fear of being forgotten at renewal time.
He avoids AI as a habit rather than a considered view.

steps.text: Pay about £40 a month into a savings account before the spring renewal
Keep checking site drawings at the Hull firm and ask Pete about renewal
Contact the engineering union about starting a branch at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than my firm is ready for. We're about to get a package that reads drawings and flags errors, and that's exactly the afternoon work they give me. At lunch I'd say the technicians will be asked to do twice as much with the tool, for the same pay. Online I'd call for rules so firms can't swap graduates for software without paying into some kind of fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my job is the easiest one to cut. My line manager Pete does the clever judgement and I do the checking. If the tool checks, then they need Pete and maybe one cheap person, and I'm not sure which of us they'd pick to be cheap. I keep thinking about the other four graduates who left this year, and none of them replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd learn the new package, grumpily, because if I don't I'm out. I'd start looking at survey work in the field, because a site needs a human with boots for a while yet. I'd cut my phone plan and my streaming, and I'd shift my loan to the longest term even though it costs more. And I'd push the union idea with the other junior staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a trap. I don't like the tool and I have to learn it anyway, and that makes me angry. Then I get scared, then I feel guilty for being scared when others have it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the package grumpily. What does that look like on a Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete would give me an hour with the vendor's training videos, and I'd sit through them with my arms folded. Then I'd test it on a drawing I already finished and see if it finds the mistakes I found. If it misses some, I'd tell Pete straight away so he knows the tool isn't magic. I'd want that on record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta (a colleague in the drawing office) who's been there nineteen years. She's the one who knows where every old pipe on the city plans actually runs. Management thinks that's replaceable once the tool has scanned the old plans, and she knows it. She's quiet and she doesn't join anything, so nobody would speak up for her.

say: I'd say the firm is **unready** and technicians will do twice the work for the same pay.
I'd argue online that firms swapping graduates for software should **pay** into a fund.
think: Privately, I fear checking drawings is the **easiest** job to cut, and mine.
Four graduates left this year and **none** were replaced.
do: Learn the new checking package, but test it against my own **finished** drawings.
Look for **survey** field work, where a person still has to stand on site.
Cut my phone plan and stretch my **loan** term to lower monthly payments.
feel: Trapped and angry about learning a tool that could **replace** me.
Guilty about being scared when others have it **worse**.
S1.quote: My line manager Pete does the clever judgement and I do the checking. If the tool checks, then they need Pete and maybe one cheap person
fieldNote: He read his own task list correctly: **checking** is the high-exposure part of his job.
Reluctance to use AI sits alongside a clear practical plan to protect himself.
He worries more about older colleague Marta than about himself, which says something about his values.

steps.text: Watch the vendor training and test the new package on finished drawings
Apply for survey field technician jobs within an hour of Hull
Cancel streaming and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Talk to junior colleagues about a staff union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster waiting for people like me, and that governments aren't ready. At work I'd say nothing, because it's my contract and I need the reference. Online I'd say the state has to guarantee a basic income now, because we're being told thinking work is gone in two years and nobody has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it ends my career before it starts. My whole degree was for thinking work: structures, drawings, calculations. If a machine does that cheaper by 2028, then what was the debt for? I'd be paying off the loan for a qualification that employers don't want, and I wouldn't even have had the chance to work long enough to prove myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd panic a bit, then make lists. I'd stop spending on anything but rent, food and the loan, and I'd move back to my aunt's spare room in Goole if she let me, though I'd hate that. I'd try to get into a trade, like an electrical apprenticeship, because robots take until about 2031 for hands-on work. And I'd join every campaign for support I could find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going. I'd be lying awake doing sums, and I'd feel ashamed that I borrowed so much for something that gets wiped out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an apprenticeship. What would you do about money during it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is tiny, so I'd need to keep a weekend job, probably in a warehouse. My flat share would have to go, which is why the aunt in Goole matters. It would be about two years of being poorer than I am now. I know that, and I'd still do it because the hands-on route buys me three extra years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd say to Pete, your supervisor, about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him straight if the firm plans to keep graduates. If he says no, at least I'd know and I could start earlier. If he says yes, I'd want it in writing, not as a promise on a smoke break. He's decent, so I think he'd tell me the truth, even if it's bad.

say: I'd say governments aren't ready and the state should guarantee **basic income** now.
At work I'd stay quiet, because I need the **reference**.
think: I think it ends my **career** before it starts.
My whole degree trained me for **thinking** work that a machine would do cheaper.
do: Cut everything except **rent**, food and the loan.
Move into my aunt's spare room in **Goole**.
Try an **electrical apprenticeship** with a weekend warehouse job.
feel: Like the **floor** going, with ashamed sleepless sums.
Ashamed of borrowing so much for something that gets **wiped** out.
S2.quote: If a machine does that cheaper by 2028, then what was the debt for? I'd be paying off the loan for a qualification that employers don't want
fieldNote: The 2-year window removes his sense of control: no savings, no family money, no plan beyond **retreat**.
His fear is about the debt as much as the job.
He weighs the hands-on route sensibly but only as a last resort.

steps.text: Stop all spending except rent, food and the loan repayment
Ask my aunt in Goole for her spare room
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship and keep a weekend warehouse job
Join campaigns demanding a basic income and sign on for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not long, but it's enough to do something. At work I'd say we should be told the firm's plan. To friends I'd say take the warning seriously, the way you would if a factory was announced to close. Online I'd push for training funds and for unions to get a seat when firms bring in this kind of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it still frightens me, just less sharply. Five years gives me time to clear some of the loan if I'm careful. But I'm not someone who picks up new things quickly, and I know it. So I'd have to push myself into something that isn't just drawing checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a savings habit now, even if it's small, aiming for three months of rent before 2029. I'd sign up for an evening course in site safety and surveying, because those lead to field work. I'd ask Pete to put me on more site visits this year. And I'd get more involved in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, which is a relief, though I don't trust the feeling. There's a dread underneath, like a cloud you can see coming slowly over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow to pick up new things. How will that show up in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep putting off learning anything on a screen. The course would be the one thing I'd do in person with other people, because I'm better in a room than watching a video alone. If it's all online I'd probably quit by Christmas. So I'd choose the one that meets on Thursday evenings at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it, if she asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum (his mother) cleans offices and she'd worry. I'd tell her I'm saving and learning a skill that works outside. I wouldn't tell her the loan figure, because she'd lose sleep over it. She's got no money to give me and she knows it, so I'd rather she wasn't carrying that.

say: I'd say five years is **short** but enough time to act.
I'd push for **training** funds and union seats when firms bring in new software.
think: It still frightens me, but five years gives me time to clear some **loan**.
I'm slow with new things, so I must push myself beyond **drawing** checks.
do: Save towards **three months** of rent before 2029.
Sign up for an evening **surveying** and site safety course that meets in person.
Ask Pete (my supervisor) for more **site visits** this year.
feel: Manageable, with a **dread** underneath like a cloud coming over the hills.
S3.quote: I'm better in a room than watching a video alone. If it's all online I'd probably quit by Christmas.
fieldNote: He knows how he learns and plans around it, which shows honest **self-knowledge**.
Time lowers panic but not worry; the debt remains the anchor.
He protects his mother from the debt figure.

steps.text: Save towards three months of rent before 2029
Enrol in the Thursday evening surveying and site safety course
Ask Pete for more site visits this year
Attend union branch meetings and recruit two colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it gives a whole generation time to retrain if governments stop dithering. At work I'd probably say little, but I'd mention that firms should plan their graduate intake now. Online I'd push for public money for retraining and for rules on how firms bring AI in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I feel almost calm about this one, but I know that's partly because it's far away. Ten years is long enough to pay off a good chunk of the loan and build a trade. I'd probably be a site engineer by then if the firm survives. The thing is, I still don't want to use AI, and I know I might not get to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my contract, save steadily, and aim to be properly qualified, like getting chartered status through the institution. I'd shift into site work and stay there, because I like it. I'd move out of the flat share in a couple of years and rent a place on my own. And I'd stay in the union, maybe even become the rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, even a little hopeful. I could imagine a life where I'm outside, doing real work, with machines doing the paper. That's better than the picture where I'm replaced next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not get to choose about AI. What if you had to use it every day by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, the way I use a calculator, and I'd treat it as someone else's tool that I check. What I don't want is to trust the software blindly. A drawing with my name on it has to be right. I'd say the same to any junior I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets in the way of the calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The debt, mostly. If rates go up, my repayments could jump and I'd be back to panic. And if my firm closes before I'm qualified, I'd have to start again with a different employer who might not want a pass degree. So the calm is real but it's built on a lot of ifs.

say: I'd say ten years lets a generation **retrain** if governments act.
I'd tell my firm to plan its **graduate** intake now.
think: Ten years is long enough to pay off much of the **loan** and build a trade.
I still don't want AI, but I may not get to **choose**.
do: Work towards **chartered** status through the engineering institution.
Move into **site work** and stay there.
Rent a place on my own in a **couple** of years.
feel: Almost calm and a little **hopeful** about being outdoors doing real work.
S4.quote: What I don't want is to trust the software blindly. A drawing with my name on it has to be right.
fieldNote: Decade-long runway moves him from fear to a **plan**; mood still depends on debt and the firm surviving.
He softens on AI only when it becomes a checked tool, not a boss.
The calm is conditional and he says so.

steps.text: Work towards chartered engineer status with the institution
Move into site-based work and stay on site
Pay extra on the loan whenever pay rises
Stand for union rep at the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, by a long way. Everything I've got, the degree, the loan, the contract, is tied to thinking work, and two years gives me no time to rearrange it. What would help is a guarantee that I won't be left with the debt if the work disappears, and training that pays a wage while I do it. A union that has my back would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age are told we're lucky to have a job at all. I am grateful, but being grateful doesn't pay the loan. A Thursday evening course, a union card and some honesty from my firm would be a start. People shouldn't have to be afraid in order to be taken seriously.

headlineQuote: People shouldn't have to be afraid in order to be taken seriously.
portrait: Liam is a 22-year-old civil engineering graduate on a one-year contract at a small **Hull** firm, with heavy debt.
He is progressive and union-minded, and **resistant** to change: he has never used AI tools and avoids them.
His real fear is the **contract** and loan, so he is anxious even when little changes.
His answers are always practical: **rent first**, then the loan, then the union.
Only a ten-year runway lets him imagine a settled life as a site engineer.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture worries him most, because his debt and degree are tied to thinking work.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee against being stuck with the **debt**, paid retraining, and a union that backs him.
